data.title: US, Russia talks on Ukraine involve oil deal tied to Kushner, Witkoff: Report
data.description:
The Trump administration’s ongoing discussions with Russia to end the Ukraine war now include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives tied to the lead U.S. negotiators, according to new reporting from The New York Times. 

U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, have been engaged in monthslong negotiations to end this four-year-long war. In September, the two men traveled to both Ukraine and Russia to reopen peace talks.

Several people with knowledge of these negotiations told the Times that Russian President Vladimir Putin introduced a substantial deal for one of Russia’s largest energy companies, Lukoil, to acquire oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world during his Sept. 5 meeting with the U.S. negotiators. 

The group behind this deal includes two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Witkoff and Kushner, as well as American investor and Trump donor Todd Boehly.

It is not apparent whether or not Witkoff and Kushner would profit from this deal, but the association has raised concerns about a potential conflict of interest in these ongoing talks. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment. 

A senior administration official told the Times in a statement that Kushner and Witkoff are helping negotiate the financial terms of this deal, which includes gas stations in New Jersey, to ensure “a substantial upfront payment and profits for the United States.”

Trump has repeatedly expressed hope that the U.S. and Russia can resume trade if a peace settlement is struck in the Ukraine war.

The conflict, which has now stretched over four years, has intensified in recent months with Russian air attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. 

Ukraine’s military has responded with long-range missile attacks on Russian oil storage and refining facilities.

data.title: GOP walks tightrope on immigration ahead of midterms
data.description:
Republicans are struggling with how to thread the needle on immigration ahead of what is expected to be a bruising midterm season in which many voters have soured on the Trump administration’s aggressive enforcement.

But the party has spent two years championing policies that resulted from President Trump running on “securing” the border, including a pledge to carry out the largest mass deportation operation in history.

Two back-to-back statements from Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) illustrate the problem.

In an interview with Politico on Tuesday, the lawmaker said immigration officers have been “dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years.”

“I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” he told the outlet.

“To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” he added, nodding to the need to “step back.”

But the next day, he walked the comments back.

“Let me be crystal clear: I support President Trump’s immigration strategy, full stop,” he wrote on the social platform X.

Trump has also acknowledged the issue.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.” 

The president’s comments come as a Thursday AP-NORC poll found Trump had a 39 percent approval rating on immigration, while recent Politico polling found divides in how the GOP rated Trump on the issue. Thirty-one percent of those polled who did not identify as MAGA said Trump’s deportation campaign is too aggressive.

Republicans are also struggling with the Hispanic voting bloc, which boosted Trump and the GOP in 2024. Signs of disapproval among Hispanic and Latino voters are particularly noticeable in Texas and Florida, as the GOP looks to keep control of Congress in November.

Twenty percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who supported Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote, according to a UnidosUS survey from this spring. Meanwhile, a September Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision poll found that 18 percent of Texan Latinos who voted for Trump said they no longer back him. 

Several conservative voices have grumbled about impacts.

Paul LePage, a former Republican governor of Maine who is now running for Congress, has bragged about being “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.” But he revealed recently that his son’s father-in-law, who he has said was living in the U.S. legally, was “being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington. That’s not right.” 

LePage, however, has largely refused to answer additional questions after his comments garnered headlines, saying earlier this week it was a “personal matter.”

In Florida, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R) saw that her district, which has one of the largest foreign-born populations of any in the country, was so disenchanted with Trump’s immigration policies that she campaigned on it.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in a September ad. In the ad, she stands in front of the White House, addressing Trump. 

She faced some pushback for her comments, including from constituents and Trump himself, who criticized the congresswoman in a dozen social media posts after the ad aired. Border czar Tom Homan also dismissed Salazar’s take.

“Give me an example where we went too far. That’s a pretty bold statement to make,” Homan told CBS News in a recent interview. 

Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R), also a vocal proponent of Trump’s immigration policies, offered tepid criticism after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers conducted enforcement operations in his home state, saying they did not sufficiently coordinate with police.

“Law enforcement officers were not given advance notice or the level of cooperation we would expect from ICE’s enforcement and removal operations. As a result, there have been mass disruptions to local communities and businesses,” he said in a statement late last month.

ICE has made changes to shift the optics around their immigration enforcement, moving away from aggressive raids that were advertised in advance on social media.

But many of the tactics remain the same. ICE officers are operating in unmarked cars and donning plainclothes — details that have prompted some migrants to flee amid confusion.

Arrests, however, are still ticking up and are increasingly likely to be carried out against those who have no criminal record and who even have immigration petitions in processing. 

ICE arrested about 50,000 migrants in both July and August — record-breaking figures.

Meanwhile, internal Justice Department data obtained by The Hill shows cases handled by the Office of Immigration Litigation have soared, with cases jumping from roughly 7,700 to nearly 9,500 since the start of Trump’s second term. Many of those are habeas petitions from the nearly 70,000 people currently held in immigration detention.

Other Republican senators said they’re hearing less from constituents about ICE now that the operations are quieter.

“Generally speaking, people want to see folks that commit violent crimes and, you know, removed from that aren’t supposed to be here, under deportation, be … taken out of the country,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.). “There’s been scrutiny on methods, and certain incidences have had some very sad results, obviously, with a couple deaths.”

“I feel like it’s calmed down in terms of what ICE is doing, and they’ve upped their training.” 

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) said he had also heard fewer concerns about ICE, although the Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association joined trade groups in Kansas and Texas in a letter last week describing the disruption recent raids have had on the industry. 

Lankford said the complaints that come to him are “fewer than I used to hear about that.” 

“But yes, I mean, we’ve always heard that.” 

Democrats, however, believe Republicans will suffer on Election Day given the unpopularity of Trump’s immigration enforcement and deportations after several fatal shootings this year.

“They’re no longer going after ‘the worst of the worst’ — they are acting like the worst of the worst,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said during a recent hearing on Trump immigration efforts.

“Trump’s poll numbers have sunk like a stone, and the majority of Americans have rejected their authoritarian police-state tactics.” 

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the Trump administration’s focus on meeting arrest quotas has backfired.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud,” she told The Hill last month after the release of record-setting arrest figures.

“But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well.”

data.title: Cornell rape accusation renews reputation trouble for frats
data.description:
The Cornell University gang rape allegation is the latest in a series of black marks for fraternities, leading critics to question why universities continue to support them.  

Fraternities, almost as old as the country itself, have been a staple at colleges for young men to come together with the stated goals of teaching leadership, community service and building friendships.  

But highly publicized incidents of sexual assault and hazing plague the groups, which could face a tough road to win back public trust. 

The alleged gang rape of a 20-year-old woman at the Chi Phi frat at Cornell in 2024 is the latest in a long list of incidents that have made the public wary of Greek life.  

A lawsuit filed last month by Jane Doe, the alleged victim who chose to remain anonymous, says on Oct. 20, 2024, she was coerced into alcohol and drugs at the fraternity and sexually assaulted by seven members.

During the alleged assault, one of the fraternity brothers sent a message to a Snapchat group for the frat saying there was “free p—-” upstairs, according to a screenshot from the lawsuit.

The lawsuit targets Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity, the victim’s own sorority and the bar that served her alcohol at the beginning of the night when they allegedly knew she was underage.

Jud Horras, president and CEO of the Foundation for Fraternal Excellence, said the men accused of sexual assault and those who saw that message and did nothing to stop it engaged in “a complete failure of membership of their fraternal obligations.”

“Expulsion from the fraternity, as well as suspension of the entire fraternity local chapter, is the exact right decisions that needed to happen,” he added.

Meanwhile, in a less publicized incident across the country, a former Northern Arizona University frat leader was sentenced Wednesday to two months in jail over a hazing incident that resulted in the death of a pledge, one of at least three people this year who died from hazing incidents at fraternities. The victim’s parents are reportedly calling for reforms to campus Greek life.

The data on hazing incidents and sexual assaults at frats is limited, with no conclusive nationwide numbers on whether the issue has become worse or how fraternities compare to other groups such as sports teams. 

But the Stop Campus Hazing Act passed in 2025 seeks to change that. Every Oct. 1, starting this year, institutions receiving federal student aid must publish their Annual Security Report and include hazing incident statistics, part of an effort to create the first national dataset showing the prevalence of hazing year-by-year.  

Elizabeth Allan, professor of higher education at the University of Maine and the founder of Stop Hazing, said her studies and interviews with students have shown her many involved in these situations don’t support hazing but feel pressured by peers or alumni to keep “traditions” going.  

“We often hear from students that it’s hard to change because the alumni of their organizations don’t support change, and they come back to campus, and they want to see the old ways … They didn’t like being hazed themselves, and then when they became a leader in the organization, they tried to change, but they were outnumbered and often felt pressure from alums who, instead of being supportive of the change, reinforced the old ways,” Allan said.  

“I think we could make a lot of headway toward prevention if students — if we could correct that misperceived norm,” she added. “If students knew, ‘Most of my peers agree with me that this is not good,’ and they would feel more comfortable speaking out.” 

It is estimated around 750,000 undergraduates are involved in fraternities and sororities across the country.

Backlash to incidents of sexual assault and hazing are often targeted at specific organizations, rather than Greek life in general.

Indiana University has placed five different frats on cease-and-desist, while Cornell disbanded Chi Phi in 2024 after Jane Doe’s rape allegation came to light.

But some argue these punishments lack the oversight that would be needed to fix more structural problems.  

“I can’t think of a fraternity that doesn’t have some level of prevention education as a core function of their required experience. I think where the opportunity exists is that that it’s got to move beyond compliance, and so what that really means is engaging in that type of education that’s designed to transform and really challenge chapter culture, as opposed to just being a box that needs to be checked,” said Jason Bergeron, executive director of the Association of Fraternity/Sorority Advisors.  

“The challenge, the real challenge for accountability is how that becomes not compliance focused, but becomes a part of really building positive chapter cultures and engaging in meaningful chapter change,” he continued. 

Bergeron said the frats that succeed in changing their culture are the ones that engage with the Title IX professionals on their campus and invited diversity, equity and inclusion staff to their spaces.  

“I think it is a really important tool in inviting people in to sort of demystify how these conversations occur and how cultural change ultimately can occur within fraternities,” he said. 

Those who support Greek life and fraternities say the negative headlines don’t represent the thousands of men who take seriously their obligation to speak out and intervene during unlawful or dangerous situations.  

“The research is actually clear: Fraternity men do a better job at intervening than men who are not in a fraternity and holding peers accountable. That being said, there was a complete breakdown of the obligations of membership in this Cornell situation, and fraternity men across North America want to see those individuals held to the highest degree possible of individual accountability as a reinforcing message of just how much disgust they have in what happened,” Horras said.  

But the long history of hazing and sexual assault leave some pessimistic that anything will fix the reputation frats have given themselves. 

“A good deal of the vitriol or the blame against fraternities seems pretty warranted to me,” said Nick Syrett, author of “The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities” and chair and professor of gender and women’s studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

“I think the problem is the university trying to impose what we would think of as perfectly rational standards from above — it’s not going to work unless the people who join the fraternities want to behave, and I don’t see much evidence that lots of men joining fraternities do want to behave. They have sought out these organizations in part because of their reputations for drinking and partying and interactions with young women. So, I think it depends on the will of people to want to do the right thing,” Syrett added.

data.title: Rove says if Paxton doesn't debate Talarico, 'he loses'
data.description:
Republican strategist Karl Rove said he believes Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) will lose his bid for Senate if he does not agree to a debate with his Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico.

“If he doesn’t debate, I think he loses,” Rove said in a Wednesday appearance at The Economic Club of Chicago alongside Democratic strategist David Axelrod. “If he debates, the question is, is he going to be able to go on the offense?”

Axelrod weighed in on Rove’s assertion, saying, “There’s a reason he hasn’t debated in 16 years. He’s not adroit.”

“You don’t need to be adroit in this,” Rove, a former top White House aide to the George W. Bush administration, responded. “The question is, does he have the guts to do it?”

The Republican strategist continued, “Because he goes into the debate and says, ‘You can say all those negative things about me … but I was cleared by the state Senate but I understand why you want to talk about that cause you don’t talk about [other issues].'”

Rove’s comment on the “negative things” Talarico would say about Paxton in a hypothetical debate was a reference to the Texas attorney general’s 2023 impeachment. State representatives voted to indict Paxton on corruption charges, but he was later acquitted in the Texas Senate.

“I don’t know if he’s got the political moxie to say, ‘My future depends on me getting into a debate and coming out the winner,’” Rove concluded.

Talarico has repeatedly bashed Paxton for not appearing in debates with him — notably challenging his Republican opponent to a Fox News debate during an interview last week on CBS.

Despite President Trump carrying the Lone Star State in each of his presidential bids, Paxton trailed Talarico by 2 points in a September Fox News poll. The Democrat’s lead was within the survey’s 3-point margin of error. 

The poll found an even wider gap in likely voters’ favorability ratings of the two candidates, with Talarico earning an 8-point net positive rating, while Paxton came in at 18 points underwater.

The president also called Paxton, whom he has endorsed, “a pain in the a—” during his stops this week in Texas and Oklahoma, acknowledging the Lone Star State’s attorney general is “a little controversial.” Though he added that the GOP Senate candidate “was at my side more than anybody” when he “was being hit by the radical left very hard.”

Trump’s visit to Texas came shortly after The New York Times obtained an audio clip in which Paxton said the president’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas “dropped our numbers.” A senior Paxton adviser called the report “manipulated nonsense.”

During the midterm convention, the president said he doesn’t “like the way Ken [Paxton] dresses,” “talks” or “looks” but called the Senate hopeful “the greatest” attorney general in the country.

data.title: Blue Dog Democrat drops 'Zyn' from campaign nicotine pouch can
data.description:
Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) dropped the word “Zyn” from a piece of campaign merchandise inspired by the popular nicotine pouch brand’s packaging after its parent company reportedly asked her to stop.

In early September, the Democrat added a puck-shaped storage tin, labeled “GLUE-ZYN-KAMP,” to her campaign’s storefront. Gluesenkamp Perez announced Thursday she had replaced the item with a different container, which still mimics the Zyn pouches’ ubiquitous circular packaging but instead reads “Marie for Congress.”

“Yes, we made more. Now with our limited-edition grille logo and hopefully fewer lawyers,” Gluesenkamp Perez wrote on social media alongside photos of the newly launched tins.

The new pocket-sized item shares the same $50 price tag as its Zyn-inspired predecessor but but now comes in two colors, green and black, and features the “Teamster Made” logo. 

The change comes after Zyn’s parent company, Philip Morris International, allegedly asked the campaign to stop selling the container.

“While we appreciate enthusiasm for our brands from legal-age (21+) adults, the product violates our ZYN trademark and the campaign must cease and desist using it,” a Philip Morris International spokesperson said in a statement provided to Oregon Public Broadcasting.

Gluesenkamp Perez is among her party’s most vulnerable incumbents ahead of November’s midterms, running for reelection in a district President Trump carried three times.

She has positioned herself as a centrist Democrat, notably voting with GOP lawmakers in September to pass a procedural rule that allowed a host of proposals — including a Russian sanctions bill opposed by Democrats — to move to the House floor.

This was the second time that month she defected from the party, drawing ire from Democratic lawmakers. But party leadership avoided imposing consequences for her behavior, as they hoped to retain her Washington’s 3rd Congressional District seat this fall.

The GOP considers the district to be one of its best pickup chances this fall, potentially helping Republicans retain their control of the House.

Her race against Washington state Sen. John Braun is a toss-up, with the Republican holding a 2-point edge, according to the Cook Partisan Voting Index.

data.title: Trump says he will attend Georgia-Alabama football game in Tuscaloosa
data.description:
President Trump announced Friday that he will be returning to Alabama next week for the University of Georgia vs. University of Alabama college football game. 

He made the announcement while in Mobile, Ala. for a rally as part of his travels to several different states to rally Republicans ahead of the midterms. 

The game is set to take place on Saturday, Oct. 10 at 7:30 p.m. EDT at Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa. The Georgia Bulldogs and Alabama Crimson Tide are currently ranked second and seventh, respectively, in this week’s AP Top 25.

Trump attended the University of Texas vs. University of Tennessee college football game in Knoxville last week. It was the first game he attended since January’s College Football Playoff National Championship when Indiana University defeated the University of Miami.

Trump has attended several sports events throughout his second term, including the FIFA World Cup finals in July and the Super Bowl in 2025.

Earlier this month he attended the Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland. 

He also hosted a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House in June.

data.title: Alito: 'I thought about' retiring at end of last term
data.description:
Justice Samuel Alito said he “thought about” retiring from the Supreme Court at the end of his last term following speculation about his potential retirement this year.

In an interview with CBS News, chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford asked Alito if he considered retiring in the face of “some pretty intense pressure from Republicans” who wanted to confirm his replacement while the GOP maintained control of the Senate.

“I thought about it,” Alito said. “Well, it’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term.”

“But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place. So that is basically it,” he continued. 

Alito added that he would “have to” continue to think about retirement every year. 

Crawford also asked whether his potential future retirement would “risk undoing all the work that you have done here at the court,” drawing a comparison to the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

“I think it’s too hard to predict. It’s too hard to predict, for anybody, particularly when you reach a certain age, what your situation will be a year from now, two years from now, and so forth,” Alito said. “And it’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

Alito, 76, has been on the Supreme Court for a little over two decades after President George W. Bush nominated him for the role, and is the court’s second-oldest justice, behind Justice Clarence Thomas, 78.

He is part of the court’s conservative bloc, alongside Justices John Roberts, Clarence Thomas, Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch. 

He shut down any notion of his retirement in August, telling the Wall Street Journal, “obviously I’m here for another term.”

Alito’s remarks followed NPR erroneously reporting that he had announced his retirement on the final opinion day of the court’s term. The report was retracted and NPR journalist Nina Totenberg apologized to Alito in a letter.

data.title: Alito: Overturning Roe v. Wade took 'courage' from Supreme Court justices
data.description:
Justice Samuel Alito said his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 alongside the Supreme Court’s six conservative justices, took “courage.”

In a preview for his interview with CBS News, Alito was asked if there was a particular decision that took courage.

“Well, the leading example is Dobbs [v. Jackson]. I think that required courage by all of the justices in the majority,” he said. “We didn’t know it at the time. We didn’t know it when we produced the draft that was leaked, but it required courage to go ahead with that because of the implications.”

“There are others. I mean, there are cases that have resulted in the loss of old friendships, that’s something that you have to live with,” Alito continued.

When asked if part of the job of a Supreme Court Justice is to lose friends, receive death threats or wear a bulletproof vest, he responded, “it’s part of the job that you’re going to displease people by making decisions on controversial matters because one side or the other is going to really dislike you because of the decisions.”

“The physical threats and the harassment represent something new in our society and something that’s quite disturbing, and I think it’s a danger,” Alito concluded. 

Over four years ago, the Supreme Court eliminated the nearly 50-year-old constitutional right to abortion and handed states authority to drastically limit or ban the procedure. 

Alito wrote in the majority opinion — which was leaked a month before it was unveiled — “Roe was egregiously wrong from the start,” adding that its precedent “had damaging consequences.”

The decision drew public outcry with protests outside the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at the time the decision marked “one of the darkest days our country has ever seen.” 

An NBC poll from 2023 found 53 percent of Americans strongly disapprove of Roe v. Wade’s overturn. 

Since then, many states across the U.S. have enacted near total bans on access to abortion with limited exceptions and imposed penalties for health professionals who aid in providing access to the procedure.

The Big Story 

How did the beltway take Trump’s AI accord?

In a deep dive, The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Mallory Wilson examine how Trump’s “self-policing” AI accord is landing in Washington as concerns mount over the tech’s safety.

© Alex Brandon, Associated Press

While Trump says industry officials can self-police, critics argue AI needs more oversight to keep development from getting out of hand — even as some described the accord as a step in the right direction.

 

One expert told us the administration’s concerns may be “sincere,” but the pledge is not a “solution” to preventing the potential risks of AI development. 

 

Several of the biggest players in the industry signed the one-page document Tuesday, which included four “layers of controls and audits.”

 

It declares that AI companies should implement “robust” internal controls over models, empower an internal crew to crosscheck controls and mediate any issues, partner with external auditors to evaluate their controls and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from the operating teams.

 

Some lawmakers, including members of his own party, expressed skepticism over the accord.

 

Sen. Josh Halwey (R-Mo.) called it a “good step” but stopped short of saying lawmakers can take AI executives at their world.

Hester Peirce, who became known as “crypto mom” at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), is bidding the agency adieu.

 

The SEC commissioner, who departs Friday after eight years in the role, was a key advocate for the industry during a period that saw Washington’s views on digital assets shift wildly.

 

“Serving this great nation at the Securities and Exchange Commission has been the honor of my professional lifetime,” she wrote in her resignation letter, which she shared to social media last week.

 

“The United States is exceptional because its unifying thread is a commitment to liberty,” Peirce continued. “A nation that elevates freedom of thought, expression, and action unlocks the great potential of its people to meet one another’s needs.”

data.title: Marines exceed 2026 recruiting goals
data.description:
Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter
{beacon}

Defense &
National Security

Defense &
National Security

 

The Big Story 

Marines exceed 2026 recruiting goals 

The U.S. Marines said they exceeded their fiscal year 2026 recruiting goals across every component and category, enlisting over 31,000 new recruits. 

U.S. Central Command via AP

The Marines brought in 31,250 new recruits, 1,672 officers and 3,503 prior-service reserve Marines in what the service branch called a “historic, department-wide rebound” in military enlistments.

 

“Our success this year is a testament to the disciplined execution of our elite recruiting force on the streets of America,” Marine Corps Maj. Gen. Walker M. Field, Marine Corps Recruiting Command commanding general, said in a statement on Thursday. 

 

“Likewise, it is emblematic of the legion of young Americans who are choosing, of their own volition, to serve this great nation of ours,” Field said. “The few young Americans who earn the title of Marine espouse the rare trifecta of physical, intellectual and moral fortitude to become elite warriors.”

 

While the Marines said the recruiting duty remains “challenging,” the 2026 landscape was the “most favorable” in the last five years, driven by “high” volume of interested applicants and “historically strong retention rates” across the Corps. 

 

Last year, the Marines recruited 30,536 active-duty and reserve enlisted Marines, just above 30,501 enlisted in 2024.

 

Other service branches all hit their recruiting goals for this year.

 

The Navy added 45,112 new sailors, while the Army brought in over 61,500 soldiers. 

 

The Air Force enlisted 31,950 airmen and 730 Space Force Guardians.

 

Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & National Security newsletter, I’m Filip Timotija — your guide to the latest developments at the Pentagon, on Capitol Hill and beyond.
